note:
The subject is `feint run` (#849): landing a client whose cloud endpoint is compiled in on the local emulator, with no sudo, no network namespace and no system mutation. Measured, not assumed: the published Scaleway Terraform provider honours HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and SSL_CERT_FILE, which is why the witness in object_storage_terraform_conformance_test.go uses its namespace as an ESCAPE CHECK rather than as the mechanism. The command therefore needs nothing privileged.

The design decision these mutations guard is that the command takes NO hostname. An earlier draft took `--forward host=target`, and the operator typing the hostname is the operator able to mistype it — a mistyped cloud host is not intercepted, it is resolved, so the run leaves for a third party carrying whatever credentials it holds, and the failure is silent because a request that reached the real cloud looks exactly like one that worked. Instead the mounted doors come from the emulator (GET /_feint/s3, validated by fetchS3) and each door's cloud authority comes from the pack in this binary, which is also the split s3.Profile requires: an instance fact may come from a report, a wire dialect may not. The set of possible targets is therefore the set of doors that exist, and there is no spelling of this command that sends traffic off loopback.

Mutation 5 carries the correction of a comment this file got wrong first: it claimed the file check held the signal relay. It does not, because the deferred removal runs regardless. Writing that down was necessary — a test believed for the wrong reason is the defect this repository measures most often.

Mutations 6 and 7 close #849's own two remaining asks. The first is the falsification that issue names in as many words: a run that forgets its cleanup. The second is why TestDoctorSeesARunInFlightAsItsOwner had to exist at all — TestDoctorTellsALeftoverAuthorityFromARunInFlight writes its own directories, so it would stay green if `feint run` stopped recording an owner altogether, and a diagnostic agreeing with a fixture rather than with its producer is a diagnostic that goes blind in silence.

Mutation 8 is the one this spec most needed and least expected. The command's first proof used curl against the bare authority, which is PATH-STYLE, so it passed while the virtual-host form every S3 client actually uses — <bucket>.<authority>, Terraform included — was refused at the allow-list and never tunnelled. The measurement that caught it was reading the existing Terraform witness, which declares the bucket authority explicitly beside the bare one. Widening the allow-list cannot widen what is SERVED: the wildcard decides only what is intercepted, and LocalTransport still refuses a leading label that is not a valid bucket name, so interception is deliberately wider than service and a nonsense bucket gets a local refusal instead of a trip to the cloud.

Mutation 9 holds a variable's ABSENCE, which is the only reason the environment is asserted as a list. An earlier draft set AWS_CA_BUNDLE on the reasoning that an S3 client would want it, and that reasoning was never measured: the published Scaleway provider hands its SDK a prebuilt *http.Client, so a CA bundle the SDK is asked to install on it has nowhere to go, and the apply died on a message about transports. Removing it made the same apply complete with 139,264 identical bytes in the local byte store. The command also strips the variable from an INHERITED environment, which is the one thing it edits of the operator's own configuration, because no value of it can help: the station's bundle does not contain this run's freshly minted authority.
